<reason>PRO built a simple, durable spine—speed is the severity multiplier on every crash, including the drunk driver's—and CON never actually dismantled it; CON's reframe ("a drunk at the limit kills; eight over usually doesn't") trades on frequency but concedes that lowering speed lowers harm for the impaired driver too, which PRO exploited. CON landed real hits (the sobriety-checkpoint remark, mapped-camera geography vs. unpredictable mobile enforcement, the uncovered network, surveillance), and PRO's answers to some of these were only partial (average-speed corridors, "bonus not dependency", a late plate-reader point in closing). But PRO's pressure question forced CON's "single digits, at best" hit-rate admission, and PRO turned that into the decisive externality arithmetic: scaling stops to find dangerous drivers means dozens of armed roadside encounters with innocent drivers per catch, which is the exact externality the motion asks about. PRO also correctly held the motion to "increasing traditional traffic stops" rather than impairment patrols, and neutralized the fines line by showing the same spiral applies to police tickets. Both sides had a clipped turn. CON argued well and made the debate genuinely competitive, but PRO's case was standing more completely at the end.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Q2 asking what fraction of routine stops uncover drunks/warrants/guns, followed by CON's honest "single digits, at best" and PRO's closing conversion of that into "twenty to fifty stops of ordinary people... a lottery of roadside encounters"—this made the externality prong of the motion concrete and hard for CON to escape, since CON's counter (roadside risk is small; camera harms universal) had already been weakened by PRO's fines-wash-out and only-photographs-speeders answers.</best_rebuttal>
